rv.q: Ruth is genuine, but is she right? Her assertion that her decisions are purely clinical are gradually undermined by what we learn of her personal life: the play allows us to understand her motives perhaps better than she does herself.
Viennese “comedy”, Professor Bernhardi. Again directed by Icke, this production is a very close replica of the original at the Almeida theatre.

And if pertinence is fine and dandy but not necessarily a prompt to engage a babysitter, know that The Doctor is also an involving, stimulating, moving, handsomely staged and exquisitely acted night at the theatre.
Icke's rigorous, visceral rethink...is a vital and immensely timely addition to the West End.
No play in the past 10 years has felt more tense, challenging, and intellectually provoking than this one.
At almost three hours, it's a long evening, yet it's a hugely rewarding one too.

In this fast-paced, digitally-driven world, the force of Icke's work has been dampened by the shifting tides of global events...But Juliet Stevenson's unquenchable, indefatigable performance is transcendent. It has to be seen to be believed.

It’s a sharp-tongued vivisection of identity politics, anchored by an astonishing lead performance from Juliet Stevenson. Like all good tragic heroes, Ruth Wolff (Stevenson,...) is first seen at the height of her powers. She’s the director of an institute trying to find a cure for dementia; they’re about to open a new building, years in the making.
